system: mixed system developed from Ottoman Empire codes (based on French law), British common law, and Islamic law

constitution.history: previous 1928 (pre-independence); latest initially adopted 28 November 1947, revised and ratified 1 January 1952
constitution.amend: constitutional amendments require at least a two-thirds majority vote of both the Senate and the House and ratification by the king

courts.highest: Court of Cassation or Supreme Court (consists of 15 members, including the chief justice); Constitutional Court (consists of 9 members)
courts.judges: Supreme Court chief justice appointed by the king; other judges nominated by the Judicial Council, an 11-member judicial policymaking body consisting of high-level judicial officials and judges, and approved by the king; judge tenure not limited; Constitutional Court members appointed by the king for 6-year non-renewable terms with one third of the membership renewed every 2 years
courts.lower: Courts of Appeal; Great Felonies Court; religious courts; military courts; juvenile courts; Land Settlement Courts; Income Tax Court; Higher Administrative Court; Customs Court; special courts including the State Security Court

citizenship.descent: the father must be a citizen of Jordan

world: has not submitted an ICJ jurisdiction declaration; accepts ICCt jurisdiction

executive.chosen: prime minister appointed by the monarch
executive.cabinet: Cabinet appointed by the monarch in consultation with the prime minister

b: Jordan is a predominantly Islamic country. Always respect local traditions, customs, laws and religions so you do not cause offence.
The police carry out random security checks. Keep ID (passport or driving licence) with you to show at checkpoints.
It’s illegal to drink alcohol on the street, but you can drink in bars, clubs, hotels and private homes.
It is illegal to possess, use or traffic drugs. If convicted, you can get a lengthy prison sentence and heavy fine.
Same-sex sexual relations are not illegal, but same-sex couples showing affection in public may cause offence. You could be arrested under other Jordanian laws. Read more advice for LGBT+ travellers.
It is socially unacceptable for unmarried foreign couples to live together. Some landlords may ask if you are married or request a marriage certificate.
It is illegal to encourage someone to convert to Christianity. You could face a prison sentence or a fine.

The Petra Archaeological Park has strict visitor opening and closing hours. You risk arrest and prosecution if you are in the park outside of these hours. Tourists have been locked in Petra overnight.
Ask the tourist office staff if you’re unclear about ticket prices and before agreeing to additional charges.
Cash machines are only widely available in Amman and other major towns and cities. Most places accept card payments.
